title: Thalamus & Hypothalamus
summary: The brain's relay station and its homeostatic control center.

lessons.title: Thalamic Nuclei & Relays

levels.kid:
In the very middle of your brain sits the thalamus. It's shaped like two little eggs side by side.

The thalamus is like a post office. Messages from your eyes, ears, skin and tongue all arrive there first. Then the thalamus sorts them and sends each one to the right part of the brain.

Only smell skips the post office and goes its own way!

The thalamus also helps you stay awake and pay attention. When you fall asleep, it slows down how many messages it sends up, so you can rest.
levels.hs:
The **thalamus** is a pair of egg-shaped gray matter masses in the center of the brain, one on each side of the third ventricle. It's often called the brain's **relay station**: almost all sensory information (except smell) passes through it on the way to the cortex.

The thalamus is divided into many **nuclei**, each with its own job:

- **VPL** (ventral posterolateral): touch, pain and temperature from the body → sensory cortex
- **VPM** (ventral posteromedial): sensation from the face, plus taste → sensory cortex
- **LGN** (lateral geniculate nucleus): vision → occipital lobe
- **MGN** (medial geniculate nucleus): hearing → temporal lobe
- **VL and VA** (ventral lateral and ventral anterior): signals from the cerebellum and basal ganglia → motor areas
- **Anterior nucleus**: memory circuits → cingulate gyrus
- **Mediodorsal nucleus**: emotion and planning → prefrontal cortex
- **Pulvinar**: attention and visual processing

A handy memory trick: **L**ateral geniculate = **L**ight; **M**edial geniculate = **M**usic.

The thalamus is more than a relay. The cortex sends even more fibers back to the thalamus than the thalamus sends up, so the two constantly talk. This loop helps control attention, sleep and consciousness. Damage to the thalamus can cause numbness, unusual pain, memory problems or even reduced consciousness.
levels.college:
**Organization.** The Y-shaped **internal medullary lamina** divides each thalamus into anterior, medial and lateral groups. Intralaminar nuclei (including **centromedian**) lie within the lamina; the **reticular nucleus** forms a shell on the lateral surface.

**Relay (specific) nuclei:**
- VPL: medial lemniscus and spinothalamic tract → S1 (postcentral gyrus)
- VPM: trigeminothalamic tracts and taste (solitary nucleus) → S1 face area and gustatory cortex
- LGN: optic tract → V1 via optic radiation
- MGN: inferior colliculus (brachium) → A1 (Heschl's gyrus)
- VL: dentate nucleus of cerebellum (via superior cerebellar peduncle) and GPi → motor and premotor cortex. Its posterior part, called **VIM** in neurosurgical terminology, receives cerebellar input and is the tremor target.
- VA: basal ganglia → premotor and prefrontal cortex

**Association nuclei:** mediodorsal (prefrontal, limbic), pulvinar (parieto-occipito-temporal association cortex), lateral dorsal and lateral posterior.

**Limbic:** anterior nucleus receives the **mammillothalamic tract** and projects to the cingulate gyrus (part of the Papez circuit).

**Nonspecific nuclei:** intralaminar and midline nuclei project widely to cortex and striatum, supporting arousal.

**Reticular nucleus:** GABAergic, projects to other thalamic nuclei rather than to the cortex; it gates thalamocortical traffic and generates sleep spindles.

**Firing modes.** Thalamocortical neurons fire in **tonic mode** (awake, faithful relay) or **burst mode** (sleep, via T-type calcium channels after hyperpolarization). Abnormal thalamocortical rhythms produce the 3 Hz spike-and-wave of absence seizures; ethosuximide works by blocking T-type channels.

**Blood supply (all mainly from the posterior circulation):** tuberothalamic (polar) artery from the posterior communicating artery (anterior thalamus), paramedian (thalamoperforating) arteries from P1 (medial thalamus), thalamogeniculate arteries from P2 (lateral thalamus, VPL/VPM), and posterior choroidal arteries (pulvinar, LGN).
levels.phd:
**First-order vs higher-order nuclei.** Sherman and Guillery distinguished **first-order** nuclei, which relay driving input from subcortical sources (LGN from retina), from **higher-order** nuclei (pulvinar, mediodorsal), whose driving input comes from layer 5 of cortex. This suggests that much corticocortical communication runs in parallel through the thalamus (transthalamic pathways), with the thalamus able to gate or synchronize cortical areas. They also separate **drivers** (large synapses carrying the main message) from **modulators** (more numerous, smaller synapses that adjust gain); in the LGN, retinal drivers make up only a small minority of synapses.

**Thalamus in cognition.** Mediodorsal thalamus appears to sustain and switch prefrontal representations in working memory and rule-switching tasks in animal studies. The pulvinar coordinates synchrony between visual cortical areas during attention. These roles challenge the idea of a passive relay.

**Consciousness.** Intralaminar and central thalamic nuclei support arousal. The **central thalamus** is a hub in the "mesocircuit" model of disorders of consciousness: after widespread injury, loss of thalamic drive to the striatum and cortex removes excitation, letting GPi further inhibit the thalamus. A case report of central thalamic DBS improving behavior in a minimally conscious patient (Schiff et al., 2007) supported this model, and small subsequent trials in traumatic brain injury have shown improvements in executive function. This remains experimental.

**Anesthesia.** Many general anesthetics reduce thalamocortical connectivity, and loss and recovery of consciousness correlate with thalamic activity, though whether the thalamus is a switch or a readout of cortical state is debated.

**Thalamic organization in humans** has been refined with diffusion-based segmentation and connectivity mapping (for example, matching each thalamic voxel to its cortical target). Nomenclature differs between atlases (Hassler versus Anglo-American terms), a real source of confusion when comparing surgical coordinates.
levels.expert:
**Thalamus as a surgical target.**

- **VIM DBS or lesioning** for essential tremor and tremor-dominant Parkinson disease. The target sits just anterior to VC (ventralis caudalis, the sensory relay, roughly VPL/VPM in Anglo-American terms). Stimulating too posteriorly into VC causes persistent paresthesias; too laterally hits the internal capsule. During awake surgery, microelectrode recording finds kinesthetic cells (responding to passive joint movement) and tremor cells firing in time with the tremor in VIM, and tactile cells with small receptive fields in VC. The somatotopy runs from leg (lateral) to arm to face (medial).
- **Focused ultrasound thalamotomy** is incisionless and monitored with MR thermometry; side effects such as numbness and gait imbalance usually improve but can persist.
- **Anterior nucleus DBS** for drug-resistant focal epilepsy is approved in the US (2018) based on the SANTE trial; the lead often passes through the ventricle to reach the anterior nucleus.
- **Centromedian DBS** is used for generalized epilepsies such as Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, with recent trials supporting it.
- **Responsive neurostimulation** with thalamic leads is increasingly used for multifocal and generalized epilepsies.

**Thalamic tumors.** In children, bilateral thalamic gliomas are often H3 K27-altered diffuse midline gliomas with a poor prognosis. Surgical goals range from biopsy for molecular diagnosis to resection of well-circumscribed lesions (such as pilocytic astrocytoma) via transcallosal, transcortical or posterior interhemispheric routes chosen to avoid the internal capsule. Laser interstitial thermal therapy is an option for selected deep lesions.

**Thalamic hemorrhage.** Usually hypertensive. Classic findings: contralateral sensory loss and hemiparesis (from capsular involvement), downward and inward eye deviation ("peering at the nose"), and frequent rupture into the third ventricle, causing obstructive hydrocephalus that may need an external ventricular drain. Watch the ventricles on CT, not just the clot.

keyPoints: The thalamus relays nearly all sensory input to cortex, except smell.
VPL = body sensation; VPM = face sensation and taste.
LGN = vision (Light); MGN = hearing (Music).
VL/VA relay cerebellar and basal ganglia signals to motor cortex; VIM is the tremor target.
Anterior nucleus (memory, Papez) and mediodorsal nucleus (prefrontal) are limbic/association nuclei.
The reticular nucleus is GABAergic and doesn't project to cortex; T-type calcium channels drive burst firing.

examples.src: A patient with essential tremor gets a lead in the thalamus; turning it up too far causes constant tingling of the fingers and lips.
examples.tr: Current is spreading posteriorly from VIM into the sensory relay nucleus (VC/VPL–VPM).

examples.src: A child stares blankly for a few seconds many times a day; EEG shows 3 Hz spike-and-wave.
examples.tr: Absence seizures generated by thalamocortical circuits; ethosuximide blocks T-type calcium channels.

lessons.title: The Hypothalamus

levels.kid:
Under the thalamus is a tiny part about the size of an almond. It's called the hypothalamus, and it's your body's boss of balance.

It works like the thermostat in your house. If you're too hot, it makes you sweat. If you're too cold, it makes you shiver.

It also tells you when you're hungry, when you're thirsty and when it's time to sleep. It has its own little clock that knows day from night.

And it talks to a tiny gland just below it that sends out hormones, special messages that travel in your blood to help you grow and stay healthy.
levels.hs:
The **hypothalamus** is a small region below the thalamus that forms the floor and lower walls of the third ventricle. It controls **homeostasis**, keeping the body's internal conditions stable.

Its main jobs:

- **Temperature**: acts like a thermostat. The front part triggers cooling (sweating, widening skin blood vessels); the back part triggers warming (shivering, narrowing vessels).
- **Hunger and fullness**: the lateral hypothalamus promotes eating; the ventromedial area promotes feeling full. Hormones like **leptin** from fat cells tell it how much energy is stored.
- **Thirst and water balance**: it senses when blood is too concentrated and triggers thirst and release of **ADH** (antidiuretic hormone), which makes the kidneys save water.
- **Sleep and body clock**: the **suprachiasmatic nucleus**, sitting just above the optic chiasm, gets light information from the eyes and sets the 24-hour circadian rhythm.
- **Hormones**: it controls the pituitary gland, the "master gland."
- **Autonomic control**: it drives "fight or flight" and "rest and digest" responses.

The **mammillary bodies** at its back end are part of memory circuits. When people have a severe lack of vitamin B1 (thiamine), the mammillary bodies can be damaged, causing serious memory problems.

During a fever, chemicals released by the immune system reset the hypothalamic thermostat higher, which is why you shiver even though you're getting hot.
levels.college:
**Boundaries.** Anteriorly the lamina terminalis and optic chiasm; posteriorly the mammillary bodies; superiorly the hypothalamic sulcus (separating it from the thalamus); inferiorly the tuber cinereum and median eminence, continuing into the infundibulum (pituitary stalk).

**Key nuclei and functions:**
- **Supraoptic (SON) and paraventricular (PVN)**: magnocellular neurons make **ADH (vasopressin)** and **oxytocin**, transported to the posterior pituitary. Parvocellular PVN neurons make **CRH** and **TRH** and regulate autonomic outflow.
- **Arcuate**: dopamine (inhibits prolactin), GHRH; **POMC/CART** neurons (anorexigenic, via α-MSH on MC4R) and **AgRP/NPY** neurons (orexigenic). Leptin stimulates POMC and inhibits AgRP neurons.
- **Suprachiasmatic (SCN)**: master circadian pacemaker, receiving the **retinohypothalamic tract** from melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells; drives pineal melatonin via a multisynaptic sympathetic path.
- **Ventromedial (VMH)**: satiety; classic lesions cause hyperphagia and obesity.
- **Lateral hypothalamus**: hunger; contains **orexin (hypocretin)** neurons that stabilize wakefulness; their loss causes **narcolepsy type 1** (with cataplexy).
- **Preoptic area / anterior hypothalamus**: heat loss, thermoregulatory set point; the **ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO)** is GABAergic and promotes sleep by inhibiting arousal centers. GnRH neurons are concentrated in the preoptic and mediobasal regions.
- **Posterior hypothalamus**: heat conservation; histaminergic **tuberomammillary nucleus** promotes wakefulness (why older antihistamines cause drowsiness).
- **Mammillary bodies**: receive the fornix, project via the mammillothalamic tract to the anterior thalamus.

**Circumventricular organs** lack a tight blood–brain barrier and let the brain sample blood: the **OVLT** (osmolarity sensing), the **subfornical organ** (angiotensin II → thirst), the **median eminence** (releasing hormones into portal blood).

**Fever**: cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF) induce COX-2 and **prostaglandin E2** near the preoptic area, raising the set point. NSAIDs and acetaminophen lower fever by reducing prostaglandin synthesis.
levels.phd:
**Feeding circuits.** Arcuate AgRP neurons are powerful drivers of feeding: activating them in mice causes voracious eating within minutes, and ablating them in adults causes starvation. Surprisingly, in vivo imaging showed AgRP neurons drop their activity within seconds of seeing or smelling food, before any is eaten, suggesting they encode a prediction about future energy state and motivate food seeking through an aversive "hunger" signal. POMC neurons act more slowly. **MC4R** mutations are the most common single-gene cause of severe early obesity, and drugs acting on MC4R (setmelanotide) treat specific genetic obesity syndromes. GLP-1 receptor agonists act partly through hindbrain and hypothalamic circuits to reduce appetite.

**Leptin resistance.** Leptin deficiency causes extreme obesity correctable by leptin, but common obesity involves high leptin with reduced response. Proposed mechanisms include impaired transport across the blood–brain barrier, hypothalamic inflammation and gliosis, and signaling defects (SOCS3, PTP1B). The relative importance of these mechanisms in humans is still debated.

**Sleep switch.** Saper's "flip-flop" model: the VLPO and the arousal systems (locus coeruleus, raphe, tuberomammillary nucleus) mutually inhibit each other, producing rapid, stable transitions. Orexin neurons stabilize the switch; without them (narcolepsy type 1) state transitions become unstable, causing sleep attacks and intrusions of REM features into wakefulness, such as cataplexy. Narcolepsy type 1 is strongly associated with HLA-DQB1*06:02, and an autoimmune attack on orexin neurons is the leading hypothesis. Orexin receptor antagonists are now used for insomnia, and orexin agonists for narcolepsy are in trials.

**Social and defensive behaviors.** Genetic tools revealed small populations in the VMH (ventrolateral part) and medial preoptic area that control aggression, mating and parenting in mice. Translating these findings to humans is uncertain.

**Hypothalamic thermoregulation** integrates skin and core temperature signals through the preoptic area, with warm-sensitive neurons now identified molecularly.
levels.expert:
**Neurosurgery around the hypothalamus is high-stakes.** The hypothalamus is small, deep and essential; injury can cause permanent obesity, thermoregulatory failure, disordered sleep, memory loss and endocrine dysfunction. Its walls form the third ventricle, so any approach to the third ventricle, suprasellar region or interpeduncular cistern risks it.

**Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV)**: the fenestration is made in the floor of the third ventricle, in the thin area of the tuber cinereum, anterior to the mammillary bodies and behind the infundibular recess. The basilar artery tip lies just beneath, so blunt perforation in the midline, just anterior to the mammillary bodies, is standard. Transient hypothalamic disturbances (electrolyte shifts, temperature changes, hyperphagia) can follow.

**Craniopharyngioma**: the classic tumor of this region. **Hypothalamic involvement** is the main determinant of long-term quality of life. Hypothalamic obesity can be severe and resistant to diet; many teams grade preoperative hypothalamic involvement on MRI and choose subtotal resection plus radiation (or cyst drainage) rather than aggressive total resection when the hypothalamus is invaded, to preserve function, especially in children.

**Hypothalamic hamartoma**: a non-neoplastic malformation causing **gelastic (laughing) seizures** and sometimes central precocious puberty. Seizures arise from the hamartoma itself, which is why removing or disconnecting it works. Options now include MRI-guided laser ablation and stereotactic radiofrequency thermocoagulation, with less risk than open resection; memory problems can result if the mammillothalamic tract is injured.

**Recognizing hypothalamic dysfunction on the ward:** temperature instability (fever without infection or hypothermia), disordered sodium (central diabetes insipidus or SIADH), altered sleep–wake, hyperphagia, and new endocrine deficits after suprasellar surgery. In children with an otherwise unexplained "diencephalic syndrome" (failure to thrive with emaciation despite normal intake, often with alertness and hyperactivity), image for a hypothalamic/optic pathway tumor.

keyPoints: The hypothalamus controls homeostasis: temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep, hormones, autonomic output.
SON and PVN make ADH and oxytocin; PVN also makes CRH and TRH.
Suprachiasmatic nucleus = circadian clock, set by light via the retinohypothalamic tract.
Lateral hypothalamus = hunger and orexin; VMH = satiety; loss of orexin neurons causes narcolepsy type 1.
Anterior = cooling; posterior = warming; fever raises the set point via PGE2.
Mammillary bodies are part of memory circuits and are damaged in thiamine deficiency.

examples.tr: Narcolepsy type 1 with cataplexy: loss of hypothalamic orexin (hypocretin) neurons.

lessons.title: The Pituitary Connection

levels.kid:
Hanging under the hypothalamus, on a tiny stalk like a cherry on a stem, is the pituitary gland. It's about the size of a pea.

The hypothalamus is the boss, and the pituitary is its helper. The boss sends little notes down the stalk, and the pituitary sends out hormones into the blood.

Some hormones help you grow taller. Some tell other glands, like the thyroid, to get to work. One helps your body keep enough water.

Because it sits right under the nerves for your eyes, a lump on the pituitary can make it hard to see things off to the side.
levels.hs:
The **pituitary gland** hangs below the hypothalamus in a bony pocket of the skull called the **sella turcica** ("Turkish saddle"), connected by the **pituitary stalk** (infundibulum). It has two parts with very different origins.

**Posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis):** really an extension of the brain. Neurons in the hypothalamus send their axons down the stalk and release two hormones directly into the blood:
- **ADH (vasopressin)**: helps the kidneys hold on to water.
- **Oxytocin**: causes uterine contractions in childbirth and milk release.

**Anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis):** a true gland that grew up from the roof of the embryo's mouth (Rathke's pouch). The hypothalamus controls it by releasing hormones into a special set of blood vessels, the **hypophyseal portal system**:
- CRH → **ACTH** → adrenal glands make cortisol
- TRH → **TSH** → thyroid
- GnRH → **LH and FSH** → ovaries/testes
- GHRH → **growth hormone** (somatostatin inhibits it)
- Dopamine inhibits **prolactin**

Most of these systems use **negative feedback**: when cortisol or thyroid hormone is high, it tells the hypothalamus and pituitary to slow down.

Directly above the pituitary is the **optic chiasm**, where nerve fibers from the inner halves of both retinas cross. A pituitary tumor growing upward presses on it, causing **bitemporal hemianopia**: loss of the outer visual fields on both sides.
levels.college:
**Embryology.** Anterior pituitary from Rathke's pouch (oral ectoderm); posterior pituitary from a downgrowth of the diencephalon (neuroectoderm). Remnants of Rathke's pouch give rise to Rathke cleft cysts and craniopharyngiomas.

**Relations of the sella.** Optic chiasm above (separated by the diaphragma sellae); **cavernous sinuses** laterally, containing the internal carotid artery and CN VI, with CN III, IV, V1 and V2 in the lateral wall; sphenoid sinus below (the route for transsphenoidal surgery).

**Portal system.** Hypothalamic releasing hormones enter capillaries in the median eminence, travel down portal veins and reach anterior pituitary cells at high concentration. Prolactin is unique: its main hypothalamic control is **inhibitory** (dopamine). So **stalk compression** by any sellar mass interrupts dopamine delivery and causes **mild hyperprolactinemia** (the "stalk effect"), while other anterior hormones may fall.

**Pituitary adenomas (now often termed pituitary neuroendocrine tumors, PitNETs).**
- **Prolactinoma**: most common functioning type. Amenorrhea, galactorrhea, infertility, low libido. First-line treatment is a **dopamine agonist** (cabergoline or bromocriptine), which usually shrinks the tumor; surgery is not first-line for most.
- **Somatotroph adenoma**: excess GH → acromegaly in adults (enlarged hands, feet, jaw), gigantism before growth plates close. Screen with IGF-1.
- **Corticotroph adenoma**: excess ACTH → **Cushing disease**.
- **Non-functioning macroadenoma**: presents with mass effect: visual loss, headache, hypopituitarism.

**Hypopituitarism**: GH and gonadotropins are typically lost first, ACTH and TSH later. **Adrenal insufficiency is the life-threatening deficit**; replace cortisol before thyroid hormone, since giving thyroid hormone first can precipitate adrenal crisis.

**Diabetes insipidus** (renamed **arginine vasopressin deficiency** in 2022 for the central form): large volumes of dilute urine, thirst and rising sodium if the patient can't drink. Treated with desmopressin.
levels.phd:
**Pituitary cell lineages.** Anterior pituitary cells differentiate under transcription factors that now organize the WHO classification of pituitary tumors (2022): **PIT1** (somatotrophs, lactotrophs, thyrotrophs), **TPIT** (corticotrophs) and **SF1** (gonadotrophs). Most "non-functioning" adenomas are silent gonadotroph (SF1) tumors. The renaming to PitNETs emphasizes that a subset behave aggressively and invade, although most remain benign.

**Feedback architecture.** The HPA axis shows ultradian pulses as well as a circadian rhythm, with peak cortisol in the early morning. Pulsatility matters: GnRH must be released in pulses to stimulate LH and FSH, whereas continuous GnRH-agonist exposure desensitizes gonadotrophs, a principle used to suppress puberty or sex hormones therapeutically. Kisspeptin neurons in the arcuate and anteroventral periventricular regions drive GnRH pulses and the preovulatory surge; mutations in kisspeptin signaling cause failure of puberty.

**Vasopressin regulation.** Osmoreceptors in the OVLT are exquisitely sensitive to small rises in plasma osmolality; volume and pressure changes act through baroreceptors with a higher threshold but can override osmotic control. Copeptin, a stable fragment co-secreted with vasopressin, is now used as a surrogate marker to distinguish central AVP deficiency from primary polydipsia, with stimulation tests (hypertonic saline or arginine) shown in recent studies to outperform the classic water deprivation test.

**Developmental genetics.** Kallmann syndrome arises from failed migration of GnRH neurons from the olfactory placode, explaining the combination of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and anosmia (genes include ANOS1, FGFR1). Septo-optic dysplasia (HESX1 and others) combines optic nerve hypoplasia, midline brain defects and pituitary hormone deficiencies.

**Craniopharyngioma subtypes** have distinct molecular drivers: adamantinomatous (children and adults, CTNNB1/β-catenin mutations, calcified, cystic with "machinery oil" fluid) and papillary (adults, BRAF V600E). Papillary tumors can respond dramatically to BRAF/MEK inhibitors, an example of molecular diagnosis changing surgical strategy.
levels.expert:
**Endoscopic endonasal transsphenoidal surgery** is the standard approach for most pituitary adenomas. The sphenoid sinus is opened and the sellar floor removed; key landmarks in the sphenoid are the carotid prominences laterally, the optic protuberances, and the opticocarotid recesses. Bleeding from the cavernous sinus or, rarely, carotid injury are the feared complications; preoperative imaging of the carotid position (including "kissing carotids") is essential. CSF leak is managed with multilayer reconstruction, often a vascularized nasoseptal flap for larger defects.

**Know when not to operate:** most prolactinomas are treated medically. Before surgery on any sellar mass, check prolactin; very large tumors can cause a falsely low result through the "hook effect" in some assays, so ask the lab for dilution when the number doesn't fit the size.

**Pituitary apoplexy**: sudden hemorrhage or infarction of an adenoma causing thunderclap headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia (cavernous sinus nerves) and acute adrenal insufficiency. Immediate steroid replacement is lifesaving; urgent decompression is considered for severe or worsening visual deficits or reduced consciousness.

**Perioperative endocrine care:**
- Assess and cover the adrenal axis around surgery; postoperative morning cortisol helps decide who needs ongoing replacement.
- Measure sodium and urine output closely. **Central AVP deficiency (DI)** often appears in the first one to two days. A **triphasic response** can follow stalk injury: early DI, then SIADH-like hyponatremia around days 5–10 as stored vasopressin leaks from degenerating terminals, then possible permanent DI. Delayed hyponatremia is a common reason for readmission, so sodium is often rechecked about a week after surgery.
- Cushing disease remission is judged by very low postoperative cortisol; acromegaly by GH and IGF-1 normalization.

**Visual outcome** after chiasm decompression is often good, especially when deficits are of short duration; optic disc atrophy and long-standing deficits predict poorer recovery. Optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fiber layer helps predict recovery before surgery.

keyPoints: Posterior pituitary releases ADH and oxytocin made in hypothalamic SON/PVN neurons.
Anterior pituitary (from Rathke's pouch) is controlled by releasing hormones via the hypophyseal portal system.
Dopamine inhibits prolactin; stalk compression causes mild hyperprolactinemia.
Pituitary tumors pressing on the optic chiasm cause bitemporal hemianopia.
Prolactinomas are usually treated first with dopamine agonists, not surgery.
After pituitary surgery watch for DI, delayed hyponatremia (triphasic response) and adrenal insufficiency.

lessons.title: Clinical Syndromes

levels.kid:
When the thalamus or hypothalamus gets hurt, the body can act in strange ways.

If the thalamus is hurt, a person might feel numb on one side. Sometimes, later on, that side starts to hurt even when nothing touches it, like an alarm that rings by mistake.

If the hypothalamus is hurt, the body's balance boss gets confused. A person might feel super thirsty and pee a lot, get too hot or too cold, feel hungry all the time, or sleep at odd times.

Doctors look for these clues to figure out which part is hurt, like detectives.
levels.hs:
Because the thalamus and hypothalamus control so much, damage to them causes recognizable patterns.

**Thalamic syndromes:**
- **Thalamic stroke**: a stroke in the sensory part of the thalamus causes numbness of the whole opposite side (face, arm and leg), a "pure sensory stroke."
- **Thalamic pain syndrome** (Dejerine–Roussy): weeks to months after a thalamic stroke, the numb side can develop burning, severe pain, and even light touch may hurt.
- **Artery of Percheron stroke**: in some people, one small artery supplies the inner parts of both thalami. A blockage can make the person suddenly very sleepy or unresponsive, with eye movement problems and memory loss.
- **Wernicke encephalopathy**: caused by a severe lack of vitamin B1 (thiamine). Classic signs are confusion, eye movement problems and unsteady walking. It's an emergency; thiamine is given right away.

**Hypothalamic and pituitary-region syndromes:**
- **Diabetes insipidus**: not enough ADH, so the person urinates huge amounts and is constantly thirsty.
- **SIADH**: too much ADH, so the body holds water and blood sodium drops, which can cause confusion and seizures.
- **Hypothalamic obesity**: damage to appetite centers, often after tumors in this region, causes constant hunger.
- **Narcolepsy**: loss of orexin neurons causes sudden sleep attacks.
- **Precocious puberty**: puberty starting much earlier than normal, sometimes from a hypothalamic lesion.
levels.college:
**Thalamic vascular syndromes by territory:**
- **Thalamogeniculate (lateral, VPL/VPM)**: contralateral hemisensory loss (pure sensory stroke), sometimes with ataxia or hemiparesis from adjacent structures; later **Dejerine–Roussy** central post-stroke pain with allodynia.
- **Paramedian (from P1)**: decreased arousal, vertical gaze palsy, memory impairment. A single **artery of Percheron** supplying both paramedian thalami (and often the rostral midbrain) causes bilateral infarcts: sudden coma or hypersomnolence. Early CT is often normal; MRI shows bilateral medial thalamic lesions, sometimes a "V sign" on the midbrain surface.
- **Tuberothalamic (polar)**: abulia, personality change and memory deficits, with language problems if left-sided.
- **Posterior choroidal**: visual field defects (LGN), variable sensory signs.

**Thalamic hemorrhage**: hypertensive; hemisensory loss, hemiparesis (capsule), downward gaze deviation, risk of intraventricular extension and hydrocephalus.

**Wernicke encephalopathy**: thiamine deficiency (malnutrition, hyperemesis, bariatric surgery, chronic alcohol use disorder, prolonged vomiting). Triad: confusion, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus, ataxia (all three present in a minority). MRI: symmetric signal change in medial thalami, mammillary bodies, periaqueductal gray. **Give thiamine before or with glucose**, since glucose without thiamine can worsen it. Untreated, it can progress to **Korsakoff syndrome** (dense anterograde amnesia with confabulation).

**Sodium disorders in neurosurgical patients:**
- **Central AVP deficiency (DI)**: high urine output, dilute urine, rising serum sodium.
- **SIADH**: low sodium, concentrated urine, **euvolemic**; treated with fluid restriction, among other options.
- **Cerebral salt wasting**: low sodium with renal salt loss and **volume depletion**; treated with fluids and salt. Common after subarachnoid hemorrhage, where fluid restriction is avoided because hypovolemia worsens vasospasm risk.

**Other hypothalamic syndromes:** Kallmann syndrome (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism + anosmia), hypothalamic hamartoma (gelastic seizures, precocious puberty), narcolepsy type 1, poikilothermia, and diencephalic syndrome in infants.
levels.phd:
**Central post-stroke pain.** Thalamic pain affects a substantial minority of patients after lesions involving the ventral posterior nucleus and adjacent regions, especially when the spinothalamic pathway is damaged. Leading hypotheses: loss of inhibitory input normally provided by the spinothalamic–thalamocortical system (the "disinhibition" or "thermosensory disinhibition" hypothesis of Craig), abnormal burst firing in deafferented thalamic neurons, and maladaptive cortical plasticity in insula and somatosensory cortex. That deafferented neurons fire in bursts via T-type calcium channels links this to the thalamic oscillation biology of sleep. Treatment responses (anticonvulsants, antidepressants, motor cortex stimulation, DBS of sensory thalamus or periventricular gray) are modest and variable.

**Fatal familial insomnia.** A prion disease caused by the PRNP D178N mutation together with methionine at codon 129 on the same allele (the same mutation with valine causes a CJD phenotype, a striking example of genetic modifiers). Pathology shows selective degeneration of the anterior and mediodorsal thalamus. Patients lose sleep spindles and slow-wave sleep, develop autonomic hyperactivity, and decline over months. A sporadic form exists. It demonstrates the thalamus's role in generating sleep.

**Thalamic aphasia and cognition.** Left thalamic lesions can cause fluent aphasia with preserved repetition and semantic paraphasias; mechanisms may include diaschisis (remote cortical hypometabolism) and disrupted thalamocortical language networks. Thalamic dementia after paramedian infarcts shows how a small subcortical lesion can mimic widespread cortical disease.

**Disorders of water balance: refined physiology.** "Reset osmostat" is a SIADH variant where vasopressin regulation works but around a lower set point. The existence and frequency of **cerebral salt wasting** as a distinct entity remains debated; some argue many cases are misclassified SIADH, because volume status is hard to measure clinically. Proposed mechanisms include natriuretic peptides and reduced sympathetic drive to the kidney.

**Hypothalamic dysfunction after injury** (traumatic brain injury, SAH) includes delayed hypopituitarism, increasingly recognized and possibly underdiagnosed, which supports endocrine screening in survivors.
levels.expert:
**Neuro ICU and neurosurgical ward pearls:**

**The drowsy patient with bilateral medial thalamic lesions.** An artery of Percheron infarct can present as unexplained coma with a normal early CT; it is often misdiagnosed as toxic-metabolic encephalopathy. Pupillary abnormalities and vertical gaze palsy are clues. Get MRI with diffusion. Top-of-the-basilar syndrome is the main differential, and it requires urgent vascular imaging because it may be treatable with thrombectomy.

**Wernicke risk in surgical patients**: prolonged vomiting, poor intake, bariatric surgery, cancer, malnutrition in prolonged ICU stays, and refeeding. Give thiamine early and generously by vein when suspected (no dosing given here; follow protocols). It is cheap, safe and preventive. Don't wait for the full triad.

**Sodium after neurosurgery** is a daily discipline:
- After pituitary or suprasellar surgery: polyuria with rising sodium and low urine osmolality suggests central AVP deficiency; confirm before treating, because postoperative diuresis of IV fluids can mimic it. Watch for the triphasic response.
- After SAH: hyponatremia is common. Distinguish SIADH from cerebral salt wasting by volume status as best you can, but treat practically: **avoid fluid restriction** in SAH because hypovolemia raises the risk of delayed cerebral ischemia. Hypertonic saline and mineralocorticoid support are used per protocol.
- Correct chronic hyponatremia slowly. Overly rapid correction risks **osmotic demyelination** (central pontine and extrapontine myelinolysis), which can be devastating.
- In patients with absent thirst (adipsic DI after craniopharyngioma surgery), sodium can swing dangerously; these patients need fixed fluid plans and close monitoring.

**Thalamic pain is a neurosurgical problem too.** For refractory central pain, options include motor cortex stimulation and DBS of sensory thalamus or periventricular/periaqueductal gray, with variable results; newer targets such as the anterior cingulate have been explored. Set expectations carefully.

**Pattern recognition**: polyuria + visual field cut + headache in a child = suprasellar mass (craniopharyngioma or germinoma) until proven otherwise. Check tumor markers in CSF and serum for germinoma before surgery, because germinomas respond to chemotherapy and radiation.

keyPoints: Lateral thalamic stroke: contralateral pure sensory loss; later Dejerine–Roussy thalamic pain.
Artery of Percheron occlusion: bilateral paramedian thalamic infarcts with coma or hypersomnolence.
Wernicke encephalopathy: thiamine deficiency; confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia; give thiamine before glucose.
Central AVP deficiency (DI): high dilute urine output, rising sodium.
SIADH is euvolemic hyponatremia; cerebral salt wasting is hypovolemic; avoid fluid restriction after SAH.
Hypothalamic lesions cause obesity, temperature instability, sleep disorders and precocious puberty.
